item.question: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm, and explain why AC and BC are both 4 cm.
steps_tex: Draw the base $AB$ of length $4\text{ cm}$.
With the compass set to $4\text{ cm}$ and the point on $A$, draw a long arc above the base.
Keep the compass at $4\text{ cm}$, put the point on $B$, and draw a second arc that crosses the first.
Mark the crossing point $C$. It is on the arc from $A$, so $AC = 4\text{ cm}$, and on the arc from $B$, so $BC = 4\text{ cm}$.
Join $AC$ and $BC$. All three sides are $4\text{ cm}$.
item.answer_tex: An equilateral triangle $ABC$ with $AB = BC = CA = 4\text{ cm}$

item.question: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm and say what kind of triangle it is.
steps: Take the side of 6 cm as the base AB.
From A draw an arc of radius 4 cm, and from B draw an arc of radius 4 cm. They cross at C.
C is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B, so AC = BC = 4 cm.
Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.
item.answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm
item.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm and say what kind of triangle it is.
1. Take the side of 6 cm as the base AB.
2. From A draw an arc of radius 4 cm, and from B draw an arc of radius 4 cm. They cross at C.
3. C is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B, so AC = BC = 4 cm.
4. Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.
Answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm

steps_tex: Each set satisfies the check: the two shorter lengths add to more than the longest $(4 + 4 > 6$, $3 + 4 > 5$, $1 + 5 > 5$, $4 + 6 > 8$, $3.5 + 3.5 > 3.5)$, so each triangle can be built.
For each set draw the longest side as the base, then an arc of one of the other lengths from each end.

$(d)$: $4$, $6$, $8$ has three different sides: scalene. $(e)$: $3.5$, $3.5$, $3.5$ has three equal sides: equilateral.
item.answer_tex: All five can be built: $(a)$: isosceles, $(b)$: scalene, $(c)$: isosceles, $(d)$: scalene, $(e)$: equilateral

item.question: A circle is drawn with its centre marked, and some points are marked on the circle. Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles.
steps_tex: Mark the centre $O$ and two points $P$ and $Q$ on the circle. Join $OP$, $OQ$ and $PQ$.
$OP$ and $OQ$ are both radii of the same circle, so $OP = OQ$ and triangle $OPQ$ is isosceles.
Choosing $P$ and $Q$ so that $PQ$ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take $P$ and $Q$, then take $R$ halfway between them on the circle, so that $RP = RQ$.
item.answer_tex: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle
steps: Mark the centre O and two points P and Q on the circle. Join OP, OQ and PQ.
OP and OQ are both radii of the same circle, so OP = OQ and triangle OPQ is isosceles.
Choosing P and Q so that PQ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take P and Q, then take R halfway between them on the circle, so that RP = RQ.
item.answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle
item.text:
$1$. Mark the centre $O$ and two points $P$ and $Q$ on the circle. Join $OP$, $OQ$ and $PQ$.
$2$. $OP$ and $OQ$ are both radii of the same circle, so $OP = OQ$ and triangle $OPQ$ is isosceles.
$3$. Choosing $P$ and $Q$ so that $PQ$ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
$4$. Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take $P$ and $Q$, then take $R$ halfway between them on the circle, so that $RP = RQ$.
Answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

item.question: Two circles of the same size have centres A and B, and each circle passes through the centre of the other. Then three circles of the same size have centres A, B and C, and each circle passes through the centres of the other two. Use the points on the circles and/or their centres to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.
steps_tex: Two circles: each passes through the other's centre, so the radius equals $AB$. Let $C$ and $D$ be the two points where the circles cross.
$C$ is on the circle at $A$, so $AC = AB$, and on the circle at $B$, so $BC = AB$. All three sides of triangle $ABC$ are equal: it is equilateral. In the same way triangle $ABD$ is equilateral.
$AC = AD$ because both are radii of the circle at $A$, so triangle $ACD$ is isosceles; triangle $BCD$ is isosceles in the same way.

Three circles: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the centres and every pair of centres is one radius apart, so triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. Each pair of circles crosses in two points, and each crossing point together with those two centres gives another equilateral triangle.
Any point on a circle with the centre and another point on the same circle gives an isosceles triangle, as in the single circle.
item.answer_tex: Triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ are equilateral, and $ACD$ and $BCD$ are isosceles; with three circles $ABC$ is equilateral and each crossing point forms more equilateral triangles

concept_name: A direct path and a roundabout path

item.question: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
steps: Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
item.answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m
item.text:
Worked example: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
1. Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
2. Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
3. 30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
4. The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
Answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

item.question: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm, and say what happens to the arcs.
steps_tex: Take $8\text{ cm}$ as the base $AB$. Draw an arc of $3\text{ cm}$ from $A$ and an arc of $4\text{ cm}$ from $B$.
From $A$, the arc reaches $3\text{ cm}$ along the base and the arc from $B$ reaches $4\text{ cm}$ back, which covers $3 + 4 = 7\text{ cm}$ of the $8\text{ cm}$. They do not meet.
For $2$, $3$ and $6$, take $6\text{ cm}$ as the base. The arcs of $2\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ cover $2 + 3 = 5\text{ cm}$ of the $6\text{ cm}$ and do not meet.
In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: $3 + 4 = 7 < 8$ and $2 + 3 = 5 < 6$.
item.answer_tex: No triangle can be built for $3$, $4$, $8$ or for $2$, $3$, $6$: the arcs never meet
steps: Take 8 cm as the base AB. Draw an arc of 3 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B.
From A, the arc reaches 3 cm along the base and the arc from B reaches 4 cm back, which covers 3 + 4 = 7 cm of the 8 cm. They do not meet.
For 2, 3 and 6, take 6 cm as the base. The arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm cover 2 + 3 = 5 cm of the 6 cm and do not meet.
In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6.
item.answer: No triangle can be built for 3, 4, 8 or for 2, 3, 6: the arcs never meet
item.text:

item.question: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm? Compare each direct length with the roundabout length.
steps_tex: Between $B$ and $C$: direct $BC = 10\text{ cm}$; roundabout $BA + AC = 15 + 30 = 45\text{ cm}$. $10 < 45$, which is fine.
Between $A$ and $B$: direct $AB = 15\text{ cm}$; roundabout $AC + CB = 30 + 10 = 40\text{ cm}$. $15 < 40$, which is fine.
Between $C$ and $A$: direct $CA = 30\text{ cm}$; roundabout $CB + BA = 10 + 15 = 25\text{ cm}$. $30 > 25$, which is absurd.
One direct path is longer than its roundabout path, so no triangle exists.
item.answer_tex: No triangle exists: $30$ is greater than $10 + 15 = 25$
steps: Between B and C: direct BC = 10 cm; roundabout BA + AC = 15 + 30 = 45 cm. 10 < 45, which is fine.
Between A and B: direct AB = 15 cm; roundabout AC + CB = 30 + 10 = 40 cm. 15 < 40, which is fine.
Between C and A: direct CA = 30 cm; roundabout CB + BA = 10 + 15 = 25 cm. 30 > 25, which is absurd.
One direct path is longer than its roundabout path, so no triangle exists.
item.answer: No triangle exists: 30 is greater than 10 + 15 = 25
item.text:
$1$. Between $B$ and $C$: direct $BC = 10\text{ cm}$; roundabout $BA + AC = 15 + 30 = 45\text{ cm}$. $10 < 45$, which is fine.
$2$. Between $A$ and $B$: direct $AB = 15\text{ cm}$; roundabout $AC + CB = 30 + 10 = 40\text{ cm}$. $15 < 40$, which is fine.
$3$. Between $C$ and $A$: direct $CA = 30\text{ cm}$; roundabout $CB + BA = 10 + 15 = 25\text{ cm}$. $30 > 25$, which is absurd.
$4$. One direct path is longer than its roundabout path, so no triangle exists.
Answer: No triangle exists: $30$ is greater than $10 + 15 = 25$

item.question: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm? Verify by construction.
steps_tex: The longest length is $7\text{ cm}$. The other two add to $3 + 3 = 6\text{ cm}$.
$7 > 6$, so the direct path of $7\text{ cm}$ is longer than the roundabout path of $6\text{ cm}$. No triangle exists.
Check by construction: take the $7\text{ cm}$ side as the base and draw an arc of $3\text{ cm}$ from each end. The arcs cover $6\text{ cm}$ of the $7\text{ cm}$ and do not meet.
Rearranging the lengths does not help: $7$ is still more than $3 + 3$.

Check by construction: take the 7 cm side as the base and draw an arc of 3 cm from each end. The arcs cover 6 cm of the 7 cm and do not meet.
Rearranging the lengths does not help: 7 is still more than 3 + 3.
item.text:
$1$. The longest length is $7\text{ cm}$. The other two add to $3 + 3 = 6\text{ cm}$.
$2$. $7 > 6$, so the direct path of $7\text{ cm}$ is longer than the roundabout path of $6\text{ cm}$. No triangle exists.
$3$. Check by construction: take the $7\text{ cm}$ side as the base and draw an arc of $3\text{ cm}$ from each end. The arcs cover $6\text{ cm}$ of the $7\text{ cm}$ and do not meet.

steps_tex: Write the lengths in increasing order: $p$, $q$, $r$ with $p \leq q \leq r$.
The length $r$ is the longest, so $p < q + r$ is true because $q + r$ is already at least $r$, which is at least $p$. Also $q < p + r$, because $p + r$ is at least $r$, which is at least $q$.
Only the comparison for $r$, $r < p + q$, can fail.

Test with $7$, $10$, $15$: $7 < 10 + 15 = 25$ and $10 < 7 + 15 = 22$ hold, and the longest check $15 < 7 + 10 = 17$ holds too. For $10$, $15$, $30$ the first two hold and only the longest check, $30 < 25$, fails.
So at least two comparisons always hold, and the two that always hold belong to the two shorter lengths. Only the longest length needs a check.

item.question: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm? Picture the circles on the longest side.
steps_tex: Check the longest length: $8 < 4 + 5 = 9$, so the triangle inequality is satisfied.
Take the base $AB = 8\text{ cm}$. Draw a circle of radius $4\text{ cm}$ at $A$ and a circle of radius $5\text{ cm}$ at $B$.
Let $X$ be the point where the circle at $A$ meets $AB$. Then $AX = 4\text{ cm}$, so $BX = 8 - 4 = 4\text{ cm}$.
$BX = 4\text{ cm}$ is less than the radius $5\text{ cm}$ of the circle at $B$, so the circle at $B$ goes beyond $X$, into the circle at $A$. The circles cross at two points.
Either crossing point with $A$ and $B$ gives a triangle with sides $4\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$.
item.answer_tex: Yes, a triangle exists with sidelengths $4\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$: the two circles cross at two points

item.question: On a base AB, take two circles whose radii are the two smaller lengths. For the sets 3, 5, 8 and 2, 5, 8 and 5, 6, 8 say whether the circles touch, miss or cross, and whether a triangle exists.
steps: 3, 5, 8: the base is 8 and the radii are 3 and 5. The radii add to 3 + 5 = 8, equal to the base, so the circles touch at one point. No triangle.
2, 5, 8: the radii add to 2 + 5 = 7, less than 8, so the circles miss. No triangle.
5, 6, 8: the radii add to 5 + 6 = 11, more than 8, so the circles cross in two points. A triangle exists.

concept_name: A complete test for a triangle

item.question: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths can make a triangle, and use it on 3.5, 6 and 9, and on 4, 7 and 11.
steps: Step 1: find the longest length.
Step 2: add the other two lengths.
Step 3: if the sum is more than the longest, a triangle exists; if the sum is equal or less, it does not.
3.5, 6, 9: the longest is 9 and 3.5 + 6 = 9.5. 9.5 > 9, so a triangle exists.
4, 7, 11: the longest is 11 and 4 + 7 = 11. The sum equals the longest, so the circles touch and no triangle exists.
item.answer: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11
